nameStory: The silver hake gets its name from its distinctly silvery, almost metallic sheen that catches the light as it swims through New England's coastal waters. This gleaming appearance makes it stand out from other bottom-dwelling fish, earning it the nickname that fishermen have used for generations.
description: The silver hake is a sleek, predatory fish found in the waters off New England's coast. It has an elongated body with a distinctive silvery coloration and belongs to the cod family, though it looks quite different from its chunky cod cousins. These fish are active hunters that chase down smaller fish and crustaceans, and they can grow to a moderate size of around 12-18 inches in length.

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Distinctive silvery-metallic sheen across the entire body that feels smooth and slippery to the touch, almost like holding a wet metal bar

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Elongated and streamlined body, much more slender than cod, with a tapered tail section that feels firm and muscular

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Large terminal mouth (opens at the front of the head) filled with sharp, needle-like teeth that feel prickly to the touch

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Two separate dorsal fins on the back and a long anal fin underneath, with soft rays that bend easily when touched

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Typically 12-18 inches long with a weight that feels substantial but not heavy, usually fitting comfortably in two hands

habitat: Silver hake live in the deeper coastal waters of New England, typically found over sandy or muddy bottoms in depths ranging from 60 to 3,000 feet. They prefer the cooler waters of the continental shelf and are commonly caught by commercial fishermen using trawl nets. Unlike many bottom fish, they often swim up in the water column to hunt, making them more active in open water areas.

seasonality.spring: Silver hake begin moving into shallower waters as temperatures warm, becoming more active and easier to catch from boats.
seasonality.summer: Peak fishing season when they're most abundant in New England waters and actively feeding, with the brightest silver coloration.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to move to deeper waters as temperatures drop, often found mixed with other cod family fish.
seasonality.winter: Move to deeper offshore waters and are less commonly encountered by recreational anglers, though commercial fishing continues.

funFact: Silver hake are such voracious predators that they regularly practice cannibalism, with larger individuals commonly eating smaller members of their own species - making them one of the few fish that literally eat their own kind as a normal part of their diet!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with young cod or pollock, but silver hake have a much more pronounced silvery shine and lack the distinctive chin barbel (whisker-like projection) that cod have. Remember: if it's super shiny and has no chin whisker, it's likely a silver hake.
contextualKnowledge: Also called "whiting" by many New England fishermen and fish markets, which can be confusing since several different fish species go by this name. The scientific name "bilinearis" refers to two faint lines that run along the body, though these are often hard to see on fresh specimens.
compareHints: Silver hake is the only member of its genus (Merluccius) commonly found in New England waters, making it unique among local hakes. Compared to other members of the cod family like Atlantic cod or haddock, silver hake are much more streamlined and silvery, with a more elongated body shape and larger mouth relative to their size.
